title: Singapore Shipping Corp orders two new car carriers for US$210 mil, may add another two
article:
Singapore Shipping Corporation has contracted Guangzhou Shipyard International Company and China Shipbuilding Trading Company to build two vessels for US$210 million as part of its fleet renewal programme.

SSC may spend up to US$400 million to acquire a total of four vessels, and has received a waiver from SGX on very substantial acquisitions.

SSC's market value, based on its last share price of 28 cents on Nov 20, gives it a market value of just below $118 million.

The company had indicated in its most recent annual report ended March 31 that around 80% of its fleet is approaching "the end of their economic useful lives".

According to SSC, the two new vessels to be built are of each 7,000-CEU Pure Car and Truck Carriers and are to be delivered on or around March 31 2031 and June 30 2031 respectively.

The vessels will incorporate dual-fuel liquefied natural gas propulsion technology, providing greater fuel flexibility and improved emissions performance compared with conventional-fuel vessels.

See also: Nordic Group secures approximately $58.3 million worth of new contracts

From left: William Zhou, president of GSI; Ow Chio Kiat, SSC's executive chairman and Lai Lihua, deputy director, specialized tonnage deptartment of CSTC/ Photo: SSC

SSC plans to fund the vessels via a combination of internal cash resources, bank financing, or even capital markets if "conditions are favourable."

See also: Lincotrade secures $81.1 mil in new contracts in 1QFY2027, order book hits $149.5 mil

"Although the car-carrier market has benefited from favourable supply and demand conditions in recent years, our decision to invest in these vessels is not predicated on the continuation of current market conditions," says executive chairman Ow Chio Kiat.

"Rather, it reflects our recognition that fleet renewal is essential to SSC’s long-term future. Ships are long-life assets, and decisions of this magnitude must be guided by a disciplined assessment of the industry’s long-term prospects rather than short-term market cycles," he adds.

title: Australian opposition calls for changes to gas reservation plan
article:
(Nov 22): Australia’s opposition coalition party has raised more concerns about the government’s plan for liquefied natural gas (LNG) exporters to increase supply to the domestic market, ahead of the legislation being voted on this week.

The government wants to force LNG exporters to reserve as much as a 20% of their supply for the local market from 2028, requiring major global producers to ensure more is available for Australian consumers. On Saturday, the government said negotiations were continuing.

Speaking on News 24 on Sunday, Susan McDonald, the shadow minister for resources and northern Australia, said she was concerned about the amount of ministerial intervention allowed under the proposed domestic gas reservation scheme.

“Legislation should not be subjective,” McDonald said. “It should be really clear and transparent, particularly if you try to encourage multibillion dollar investments to extract cash resources from under the ground.”

McDonald also highlighted worries about reciprocal responsibilities, clarity around the carve-out for the state of Western Australia and the issue of oversupply in the market. “The risks of getting this wrong, particularly for the domestic companies in the south of the country is very great,” she said.

The oil and gas sector has strongly opposed key elements of the planned reform including requiring exporters to sell gas below cost, which has been backed by unions and business groups.Despite being one of the world’s biggest LNG exporters, Australia faces a shortfall on its more densely populated eastern coast towards the end of this decade. The government’s legislation is designed to help address the deficit and to shield domestic consumers from high international prices.

See also: South Korea to ground flights, delay trading for college exam

McDonald said she had been working with the government on “a very tight range of issues” and that she was optimistic they could be resolved this week.

title: China’s US$1.7 tril AI rout turns hot trade into losing bet
article:
(Nov 22): China’s AI stock trade, once a hot bet as the nation’s technology powerhouses raced to catch up with the US, has morphed into a losing strategy.

Stocks listed on three tech-focused indexes have shed a combined US$1.7 trillion in market value since the end of June, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Multifold gains in the first half of the year that pushed the likes of upstart model developer Z.AI Co and optical module maker Zhongji Innolight Co to record highs have quickly faded.

The unraveling of the global AI boom has hit China particularly hard, as frothy valuations and reliance on policy support left stocks vulnerable once cracks emerged. The appeal of Chinese AI as an affordable alternative to pricier US models and the nation’s pursuit of a self-sufficient chip chain is also being tested as the US tightens restrictions on technology exports.

The market is set for another turbulent session on Monday, after anxiety over the the viability of the AI trade turned into a full-blown rout in the US. A KraneShares exchange-traded fund tracking China’s Star 50 gauge fell more than 4% in US trading.

“As a China fund manager, experiencing this year’s wild swings and second-half selloff has honestly left us pretty speechless,” said Bush Chu, investment director of China equities at Aberdeen Investments. “Investors are worried both about an AI capex slowdown and whether US-China supply chain business is sustainable.”

See also: Abu Dhabi’s MGX gains US$20 bil from Anthropic’s listing

It’s a painful reckoning for investors who chased China’s AI rally as the “DeepSeek moment” stunned the world. The three key Chinese tech indexes are now all showing losses on the year while major peers in the US, Taiwan and South Korea remain in positive territory.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Tech Index, home to major internet names including Alibaba Group Holding Ltd and Tencent Holdings Ltd, has slumped to a two-year low. The onshore ChiNext Index, dominated by tech hardware firms, reached a record high this summer but is now down 31% on the year. The chip-heavy Star 50 Index has similarly wiped out a record rally.

See also: Ubisoft shares plummet after rival games seen hitting sales

DeepSeek introduced the idea that China’s tech firms could deliver globally competitive AI more cheaply than US majors. Technological breakthroughs from the likes of Huawei Technologies Co drove increased bets on local players, with a push from Beijing’s drive for national tech self-sufficiency.

While China has offered full support for its homegrown tech champions, the latest move from Washington could hamper their efforts. Draft rules released by the US earlier this month effectively block Chinese firms from renting cutting-edge processors from Nvidia Corp and others via overseas data centers, closing a vital backdoor for training next-generation models.

That could further impede the progress of Chinese AI, which has already shown signs of slipping. None of the current 10 most advanced models in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index are from China, a stark contrast with just four months ago when Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 was rivaling the performance of offerings from OpenAI and Anthropic PBC.

Tencent’s management warned in last week’s earnings call that the next version of its HY4 model could be delayed by the chip crunch, though it sees the domestic supply chain helping fill the gap over time. Alibaba said Thursday that it expects its cloud sales growth to slow to 30% to 45% next year before bouncing back to 50%-plus in 2028.

Chinese internet giants are also suffering from the same high AI development costs that are pressuring earnings at US hyperscalers. Sluggish domestic consumption and on-and-off price wars remain persistent worries as well.

“The key issues are weak AI monetization, compute bottlenecks, intense competition and margin pressure,” said Nick Ferres, chief investment officer at Vantage Point Asset Management. “Clearly the escalation in US tech and compute curbs adds another dimension to the downside pressure.”

On the bright side, China’s semiconductor industry has been seen as a potential beneficiary in the rush to fill the void caused by US regulations. Local foundries like Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp. in particular may see more business, amid reports that overseas manufacturers could reject orders.

Nvidia designed about a third of the chips used by China’s tech firms in the first half of this year, followed by about 29% for Huawei and 22% for Cambricon Technologies Corp., according to a report from Nomura Holdings Inc.

Valuations have dropped for Chinese tech stocks overall on the selloff, though the large Hong Kong-listed internet firms remain far cheaper than mainland hardware names. Alibaba is now trading at just 10 times forward earnings estimates while onshore shares of chipmaker SMIC are still at 80 times.

“At current price levels, I still can’t find value in these Chinese AI-related names,” said Jian Shi Cortesi, a fund manager at GAM Investment Management in Zurich. “Many stocks will need to fall another 30% to 50% to become very attractively valued.”
